title: Interplay between Excitability and Noise in Analog Spiking Neurons
authors: Léopold Van Brandt, Alon Ascoli, Michele Bonnin, Grégoire Brandsteert, Denis Flandre, Jean-Charles Delvenne
abstract: A spiking neuron is a dynamical system exhibiting a limit cycle (a spike) when subject to sufficiently excitatory input. Famous neuroscience experiments by Bryant and Segundo as well as Mainen and Sejnowski revealed that the spike times of some biological neurons are more reliable when subject to time-varying stimuli compared to constant ones. Provided with an industrial physics-based transient noise SPICE simulation framework compatible with foundry transistor compact models, we have demonstrated similar behaviours for a CMOS analog spiking neuron designed for neuromorphic computing hardware platforms. Under constant excitation current, the neuron operates in oscillatory regime and the empirical periods (interspike intervals) suffer from accumulated phase noise (jitter) during successive cycles, mainly due to the thermal noise of transistors. A time-varying input is reported to be capable of triggering output spikes according to a controlled statetransition mechanism, thereby significantly reducing the spike time jitter in the excitability regime. The physical limitation of the oscillatory or rate-coding regime in terms of reliabilitydissipation tradeoff is further evidenced by a stochastic thermodynamic uncertainty relation, a theorem that applies to general overdamped dissipative stochastic dynamical systems.
summary: This work simulates and analyzes the noise effects on CMOS analog spiking neurons, demonstrating that time-varying inputs improve spike timing reliability compared to constant inputs. By applying stochastic thermodynamics, the authors establish a fundamental physical limit (the TUR) that governs the trade-off between signal precision and energy dissipation in these artificial systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental interplay between noise and excitability in analog spiking neurons, specifically analyzing how input stimuli affect the reliability and jitter of spike timing.
main_result: Time-varying inputs significantly reduce spike time jitter compared to constant excitation, and the analysis uses the Stochastic Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR) to establish a fundamental reliability-dissipation tradeoff.
method: The study employs industrial physics-based transient noise SPICE simulations combined with theoretical tools from stochastic thermodynamics, such as the TUR.
model_or_system: The physical system is a CMOS analog spiking neuron modeled after the Morris-Lecar system, designed for neuromorphic hardware. The analysis compares its behavior under constant vs. time-varying external stimuli.
key_observables: Spike time jitter (phase noise), spike time reliability, dissipated energy ($E_{	ext{dissip}}$), and the empirical frequency ($N/t$).
important_parameters: Constant vs. time-varying input current, temperature ($kT$), and the fundamental limit set by the TUR.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of stochastic thermodynamics principles, though it notes the TUR may not apply to the non-stationary excitability regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the CMOS neuron's operation in both oscillatory (high jitter) and excitability (low jitter) regimes under different input currents, alongside plots comparing accumulated jitter over time.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from simulating the physical behavior of the neuron under different noise conditions, quantifying jitter accumulation, and culminating in a theoretical analysis using the TUR to place fundamental limits on the achievable precision.
why_interesting: The application of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics tools like the TUR to analyze the operational limits of artificial neural circuits provides a powerful, physics-grounded constraint on computational efficiency and reliability.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Diagram of an ultra-low-power CMOS analog spiking neuron based on a simpliﬁed Morris-Lecar model [4]. The input is the excitatory current iex, while the output is the node voltage vGK.

Fig. 2: Reliability of spike timing in a rat neocortical neuron stimulated by (A) a constant supra-threshold current pulse; (B) a time-varying current (frozen ﬁltered white Gaussian noise added to a constant component). Raster plots of the spike times for 25 consecutive trials are depicted at the bottom, for both experiments. Reprinted from [12] with permission from the AAAS.

Fig. 3: CMOS analog neuron in oscillatory regime under a constant excitation current pulse of supra-threshold ampli- tude 20 pA. (a) Output spikes. (b) Input excitation current iex(t). (c) Raster plot of the spike times. Simulation parameters: time step ∆t = 1 ns, intrinsic tran- sistor noise bandwidth fmax = 500 MHz. 1000 trials were performed; only 25 are shown.

Fig. 4: CMOS analog neuron excited by frozen ﬁltered white Gaussian noise, ﬂuctuation around a constant current pulse of sub-threshold amplitude 5 pA. Input noise parameters: standard deviation σiex = 20 pA, ﬁlter time constant τ = 5 µs. (a) Output spikes. (b) Input excitation current iex(t). (c) Raster plot of the spike times. Same simulation parameters as in Figure 3.

Fig. 5: Analysis of the trial-to-trial variability in the spike times for the two types of input current, respectively trigger- ing the oscillatory (Figure 3, with mean inter-spike interval or spike period E{Tn −Tn−1} ≈32 µs) and excitability (Figure 4) behaviours. The jitter only accumulates over time for the former. The variance was estimated from 1000 trials. As discussed in the text, the variances of the 4th and 15th spike times of Figure 4 are very large (20 and 8 (µs)2) and go off the scale of the plot.
